clue.text: Some advice to one imprisoned very quietly?

indicators.note: the word one holds the other pieces locked up inside it, as a prisoner is held

parts.note: taken as written
a tip is a piece of advice
taken as written

explanation.surface: A friendly word of advice whispered to a prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: The split is the trick: 'advice to' gives the inner pieces and 'one imprisoned' says the word one holds them, so the prisoner is not a person at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone creeping about on the balls of their feet moves very quietly, so the idiom means silently.

clue.text: Stops working in this direction, taking seats

parts.note: this is a down clue, so its own direction is down
stools are seats

explanation.surface: Someone stops work by moving downwards and sitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in this direction' refers to the grid: the answer is written downwards. 'taking' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: To down tools is the idiom for workers striking or ceasing work.

clue.text: Estimate another tail pinned on donkeys?

parts.note: asses are donkeys
a second copy of the last letter of the word for donkeys

explanation.surface: A party game of pinning the tail on the donkey, with one tail too many.
explanation.walkthrough: The donkeys' word ends in S; 'another tail' adds one more S at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess something is to evaluate or judge its value, a synonym of estimate.

clue.text: Pianist Spooner's given to Rent-a- Bungle?

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the starting sounds of words, so the opening sounds here change places

parts.note: to rent is to hire, giving hire a
a mess is a bungle

explanation.surface: A hire firm whose name suggests things go wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of 'hire a mess' and you hear the name of the British pianist Dame Myra Hess, famous for wartime National Gallery concerts.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Myra Hess was a celebrated British concert pianist.

clue.text: Not much required to read Riot Act

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words of the phrase, read straight through

explanation.surface: Reading someone the riot act takes little effort.
explanation.definitionFit: An iota is a tiny amount, from the smallest Greek letter.

clue.text: He gambles with more skill

explanation.surface: A gambler is the more skilful player.
explanation.definitionFit: One who bets is a gambler; the comparative of good also means more skilful.

clue.text: Dope working as diplomat?

parts.note: in means on or working, as in in operation
a diplomat works in the FO, the Foreign Office

explanation.surface: Asks whether a dope could serve as a diplomat.
explanation.walkthrough: FO is the Foreign Office, the British government department of diplomats. 'Dope' is slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: Dope is slang for inside information, the same as info.

clue.text: Sausage (spicy) the Spanish put back in place of expensive tastes?

indicators.note: these letters are taken out and placed at the very back of the rest

parts.note: a saveloy is a spicy British pork sausage
hot means spicy
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Instructions for serving a spicy sausage in a smart restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put back' moves the Spanish article from inside the sausage to the very end. A saveloy is a red British sausage; the Savoy is a grand London hotel famous for fine dining.
explanation.definitionFit: The Savoy is a luxurious London establishment known for costly dining.

clue.text: One who's vanquished lord about to interrupt catcall? WE will represent his sentiments

parts.note: the one who has beaten an opponent is the victor

indicators.note: the two short pieces break into the cat noise, splitting it

parts.note: mew is the call a cat makes
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A conquering nobleman heckles, and we speak for him.
explanation.walkthrough: WE stands for West and East: the unchecked letters down the grid's left and right edges spell the character's catchphrase 'I don't believe it'. Victor Meldrew is the grumpy hero of the British sitcom One Foot in the Grave.
explanation.definitionFit: The grid's outer columns spell this sitcom grouch's famous exasperated line, so those sides voice his feelings.

clue.text: This girl and I perplexed by Geordieland?

indicators.note: confused, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

parts.note: Geordies come from Tyneside in the North East, abbreviated NE

explanation.surface: Someone baffled by the north-east of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perplexed' jumbles AND I into DIAN. Geordies are people from Newcastle, in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Dianne is a girl's name, which 'This girl' asks for.

clue.text: Bread and butter conversation covers the writer

indicators.note: the talk word wraps around the other pieces like a lid

parts.note: a chat is a conversation
a pat is a small portion of butter
the writer of the clue refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: Bread and butter are discussed while the author is around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread and butter' looks like one phrase, but 'Bread' is the definition and 'and' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapatti is an unleavened Indian flatbread.

clue.text: Love bird is possible reason for discomfort in audition

definitions.text: possible reason for discomfort in audition

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
a tit is a small bird
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lovebird might cause trouble at a singing audition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'audition' here means hearing, not a tryout.
explanation.definitionFit: Otitis is ear inflammation, which can cause pain or impair hearing.

clue.text: Dominated on account of wearisome chap

parts.note: over can mean concerning, as in a row over money
a bore is a tedious person

explanation.surface: Someone was overshadowed because of a dull man.
explanation.definitionFit: Overbore is the past tense of overbear, to dominate or overwhelm.

clue.text: Newspaperman has written about chancellor leaving, fed up

indicators.note: the other words are written around the newspaperman, enclosing him

parts.note: Gordon Brown was the UK Chancellor of the Exchequer
off means leaving, as in I'm off
ed is short for editor

explanation.surface: A journalist reports on a finance minister departing, and is weary of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Brown was Britain's finance minister (Chancellor of the Exchequer) when this was set in 2007; 'written about' means the editor is enclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: Browned off is British slang for annoyed or weary, the same as fed up.

clue.text: Humane Romans wouldn't normally take him to heart

definitions.text: Humane Romans wouldn't normally take him to heart

indicators.note: the name sits at the heart of the two words, spanning their join

explanation.surface: Kind-hearted Romans would not take kindly to a particular person.
explanation.walkthrough: The emperor sits in the middle of 'humaNE ROmans'; as a whole, the clue says decent Romans would hardly love such a cruel ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: Nero was a cruel Roman emperor, unlikely to be loved by kind Romans.

clue.text: More than one 26 is covering mass in tar

definitions.note: the definition is plural: several feet of verse

indicators.note: the word is wraps around the other letters

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the mass letter is placed inside the sailor

parts.note: a tar is a sailor, AB for able seaman
M is the symbol for mass

explanation.surface: Something is coated with tar, with a mass inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is FOOT, a unit of verse; 'tar' is a sailor, AB.
explanation.definitionFit: An iamb is a metrical foot of an unstressed then stressed syllable.

clue.text: Fearfully having changed sides on a plane?

indicators.note: right changes to left, so the R becomes an L

parts.note: in fright means fearfully

explanation.surface: A nervous flyer has switched seats on an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: R and L stand for right and left; swapping the R of IN FRIGHT for L gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In-flight describes things happening aboard an aircraft during a journey.

clue.text: Norwegian having nothing to go on?

parts.note: O is the shape of zero
a lav is a toilet, where one goes

explanation.surface: A Norwegian has no evidence to proceed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go' is a toilet euphemism; LAV is short for lavatory. 'on' just places LAV after O.
explanation.definitionFit: Olav was the name of several kings of Norway.

clue.text: Revolutionary German air written about injurious influence having confidence

indicators.note: the reversed word is written around the corrosion word
turned round, so the German word is read backwards

parts.note: luft is German for air
rust is a corroding influence

explanation.surface: A rebellious German song about harm somehow inspires confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' turns the German word round to TFUL, and 'written about' wraps that around the corrosion; the surface's rebel song is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Trustful means trusting, ready to place confidence in others.

clue.text: With plenty, arrive home carrying list of names

indicators.note: in a down clue the home word carries the list on top of it

parts.note: a roll is a register of names
in means at home

explanation.surface: Someone well off comes home with a register.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' works for a down entry: IN bears ROLL above it.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that roll in arrive in large quantities, as money rolls in.

clue.text: Part played by polyglot on "Guess the Language"?

indicators.note: a part of the words is taken, read straight through

explanation.surface: A multilingual contestant on a quiz show about languages.
explanation.definitionFit: Tongue is an old word for a language, as in mother tongue.

clue.text: Sound quality of British Rail — eventually?

indicators.note: the clue reads British Rail in time, so the rail letters sit inside the time word

parts.note: eventually means in time, which supplies time and tells you to put something in it
BR is the abbreviation for British Rail, the old national railway

explanation.surface: Trains will get there in the end, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: British Rail was the old UK railway, known for delays. 'eventually' means 'in time': it gives TIME and says BR goes in it, so 'British Rail eventually' is 'BR in time'.
explanation.definitionFit: Timbre is the tonal colour of a sound that tells instruments apart.

clue.text: Literary landscaper turns on one more disgraced

parts.note: Blott is the gardener in Tom Sharpe's novel Blott on the Landscape

indicators.note: the two following pieces are read backwards

parts.note: re means on or concerning
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A gardener from fiction turns on someone more shamed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' reverses RE + I to IER. Blott on the Landscape is a comic novel, so Blott is a fictional landscaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A blot is a stain on one's reputation, so blottier means more stained or disgraced.

clue.text: One pulling strings and rank?

explanation.surface: A puppeteer and his rank.
explanation.definitionFit: One who ties knots pulls strings tight; a tier is a row or level in a hierarchy.

clue.text: Powerful Italian family supplying 75% of drugs

indicators.note: six of the eight letters of the medicine word are kept, counting from the front

parts.note: medicine means drugs

explanation.surface: A Mafia-style family dealing in most of the drug supply.
explanation.walkthrough: MEDICINE has eight letters; 75% of it is the first six.
explanation.definitionFit: The Medici were the rich ruling dynasty of Renaissance Florence.

clue.text: In the wars, where one is general

indicators.note: battered about, so the letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: In wartime, wherever you go, someone is in command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the wars' means injured; it scrambles WHEREONEIS. Eisenhower was the Allied supreme commander in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwight Eisenhower was a US Army general before becoming president.

clue.text: Pay former Labour leader

explanation.surface: Paying a past Labour party leader.
explanation.definitionFit: To foot the bill is to pay it; Michael Foot led the Labour Party from 1980 to 1983.
